subject: standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling

messages.author: 9ea95ff2561a8857
messages.subject: standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling
parts:
Hello,

I am fitting a toy linear mixed model with a single random generic component, y = Z u + e, with u ~ MVN(0, sigma_a^2 A), where A is known:
fit <- remlf90(fixed=y ~ 1, generic=list(geno.add=list(model.matrix(~ dat$geno.add - 1), A)), data=dat, method="ai")

With the commands "summary(fit)" and "sqrt(diag(fit$reml$invAI))", I can see that standard errors of the variance components are the square roots of the diagonal of the inverse of the observed information matrix. However, it is known (see here) that this way of calculating std errors isn't suitable for variance components whose std errors often happen to be asymmetric.

The R package "lme4" allows to estimate the standard errors of variance components via likelihood profiling. Is it available in breedR? Isn't it what is already described in this wiki page as "simulation from the asymptotic Gaussian joint sampling distribution of the variance components" citing Meyer and Houle (2013)? If yes, could it be made available for generic variance components?

Cheers,
Tim

With the commands "summary(fit)" and "sqrt(diag(fit$reml$invAI))", I can see that standard errors of the variance components are the square roots of the diagonal of the inverse of the observed information matrix. However, it is known (see here) that this way of calculating std errors isn't suitable for variance components whose std errors often happen to be asymmetric.

True. It is a common (for simplicity) approximation.
Often a bad one. But if variances are high enough, it is fine for most purposes.
The R package "lme4" allows to estimate the standard errors of variance components via likelihood profiling. Is it available in breedR?
No, it is not. You need to make ML inference for that, since it is based on a LRT statistic.
Isn't it what is already described in this wiki page as "simulation from the asymptotic Gaussian joint sampling distribution of the variance components" citing Meyer and Houle (2013)?
No, it is not the same procedure. But has the same purpose.
If yes, could it be made available for generic variance components?

It is available. See case 2.1. You need to manually specify you formula for heritability using `se_covar_function`.

Let me know if it works, or if you need any help.
I am aware that the specification of the formula is not precisely "user-friendly" :)

ƒacu.-

messages.author: 37c4b6bc71d5d203
messages.subject: Re: [breedR] standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling
parts:
No silly questions here.

What happens is that when you ask for profile confindence intervals for a model fitted with REML is that ir refits the model using ML behind the scenes, and then computes the confindence intervals for the ML estimators (see http://lme4.r-forge.r-project.org/lMMwR/lrgprt.pdf, section 1.5.1).

You can see this with a simple experiment:

 ## REML fit
 fm01 <- lmer(Yield ~ 1|Batch, Dyestuff, REML = TRUE)

 ## REML estimates of variance components
 VarCorr(fm01)   # Note sigma_Batch ~ 42
 #>  Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
 #>  Batch    (Intercept) 42.001  
 #>  Residual             49.510

 ## (narrow) profile confidence intervals
 confint(fm01, method = "profile", optimizer = "Nelder_Mead", level = 0.01)
 #> Computing profile confidence intervals ...
 #>                 49.5 %     50.5 %
 #> .sig01        37.07679   37.44472
 #> .sigma        49.42067   49.59980
 #> (Intercept) 1527.27821 1527.72179

 ## Note how the confidence interval for Batch (.sig01) is around 37.2
 ## Guess what is the ML estimate of Batch?
 VarCorr(lmer(Yield ~ 1 | Batch, Dyestuff, REML = FALSE))
 #>  Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
 #>  Batch    (Intercept) 37.26   
 #>  Residual             49.51

So, to recap. Likelihood-profiled confidence intervals are based on Likelihood Ratio Tests, which in turn require ML inference. Thus, I can’t provide profile CIs in breedR because I can only perform REML inference. Alternatively, you can use the simulation approach that you mentioned before, in order to avoid the (admittedly) inaccurate estimates of Standard Errors for variance parameters.

ƒacu.-

messages.subject: Re: [breedR] standard error of generic variance components via likelihood profiling
parts:
Thanks Vincent!

They indeed discuss bootstrapping, but emphasize that it is "prohibitively time-consuming". That's where they innovate, in "developing a fast analytical approximation depending only on the eigenvalues of the kinship matrix".

Unfortunately, they only looked at the model most-often used by human geneticists, y = X beta + Z u + e with u ~ MVN(0, sigma_u^2 K) and e ~ MVN(0, sigma^2 I), whereas animal/plant geneticists often need other random effects. Their analytical approx may not be (easily) extendable to such cases.

Anyway, for the moment I gather from all this that the solution from Meyer and Houle (2013), available in breedR via "se_covar_function", is a quick(er) alternative to bootstrap.

Facu, is there a way to change the number of samples used by "se_covar_function". I see in the AIREMLF90 manual that we can use "samples_se_covar_function <n>", but I guess it is not (yet) available via breedR? Should I create an issue as a "low priority enhancement"?

Le mercredi 28 septembre 2016 11:01:48 UTC+2, ƒacu.- a écrit :
Thanks Vincent, it is indeed relevant.

I have just gave a quick scan, and I believe that the proposed method is
very similar to the approach implemented into breedR (i.e. bootstrapping

> Le 27/09/2016 à 14:38, Timothée Flutre a écrit :
>> Thanks a lot! I read Bates' book a while ago and forgot about it.
>> After reading it again (as well as looking at your example below), I
>> understand why one wants to use REML to estimate variance components,
>> and why one has to use ML to get confidence intervals via likelihood
>> profiling. In the end, it seems strange to end up reporting a REML
>> estimate for a varcomp along its ML intervals. But I guess it is a
>> small detail often ignored in practice.
>>
>> Le vendredi 23 septembre 2016 13:39:36 UTC+2, ƒacu.- a écrit :
>>
>>     No silly questions here.
>>
>>     What happens is that when you ask for profile confindence
>>     intervals for a model fitted with REML is that ir *refits* the
>>     model using ML *behind the scenes*, and then computes the
>>     confindence intervals for the ML estimators (see
>>     http://lme4.r-forge.r-project.org/lMMwR/lrgprt.pdf
>>     <http://lme4.r-forge.r-project.org/lMMwR/lrgprt.pdf>, section 1.5.1).
>>
>>     You can see this with a simple experiment:
>>
>>     |## REML fit fm01 <- lmer(Yield ~ 1|Batch, Dyestuff, REML = TRUE)
>>     ## REML estimates of variance components VarCorr(fm01) # Note
>>     sigma_Batch ~ 42 #> Groups Name Std.Dev. #> Batch (Intercept)
>>     42.001 #> Residual 49.510 ## (narrow) profile confidence
>>     intervals confint(fm01, method = "profile", optimizer =
>>     "Nelder_Mead", level = 0.01) #> Computing profile confidence
>>     intervals ... #> 49.5 % 50.5 % #> .sig01 37.07679 37.44472 #>
>>     .sigma 49.42067 49.59980 #> (Intercept) 1527.27821 1527.72179 ##
>>     Note how the confidence interval for Batch (.sig01) is around
>>     37.2 ## Guess what is the ML estimate of Batch?
>>     VarCorr(lmer(Yield ~ 1 | Batch, Dyestuff, REML = FALSE)) #>
>>     Groups Name Std.Dev. #> Batch (Intercept) 37.26 #> Residual 49.51 |
>>
>>     So, to recap. Likelihood-profiled confidence intervals are based
>>     on Likelihood Ratio Tests, which in turn require ML inference.
>>     Thus, I can’t provide profile CIs in breedR because I can only
>>     perform REML inference. Alternatively, you can use the simulation
>>     approach that you mentioned before, in order to avoid the
>>     (admittedly) inaccurate estimates of Standard Errors for variance
>>     parameters.
>>
>>     ƒacu.-
>>
>>     El 22/09/2016 a las 17:16, Timothée Flutre escribió:
>>
>>>     Thanks for your quick answer!
>>>
>>>     About likelihood profiling, I don't have a clear idea why you
>>>     say we can't use it for variance components. Do you mean that
>>>     using REML=TRUE in lmer and then method="profile" in
>>>     confint.merMod is a mistake? Sorry if my question sounds silly.

>>>     Le jeudi 15 septembre 2016 17:44:17 UTC+2, ƒacu.- a écrit :

>>>         Hi Tim,

>>>         El 15/09/2016 a las 14:22, Timothée Flutre escribió:
>>>>         Hello,
>>>>
>>>>         I am fitting a toy linear mixed model with a single random
>>>>         generic component, y = Z u + e, with u ~ MVN(0, sigma_a^2
>>>>         A), where A is known:
>>>>         fit <- remlf90(fixed=y ~ 1,
>>>>         generic=list(geno.add=list(model.matrix(~ dat$geno.add -
>>>>         1), A)), data=dat, method="ai")
>>>>
>>>>         With the commands "summary(fit)" and
>>>>         "sqrt(diag(fit$reml$invAI))", I can see that standard
>>>>         errors of the variance components are the square roots of
>>>>         the diagonal of the inverse of the observed information
>>>>         matrix. However, it is known (see here
>>>>         <http://glmm.wikidot.com/faq>) that this way of calculating
>>>>         std errors isn't suitable for variance components whose std
>>>>         errors often happen to be asymmetric.
>>>         True. It is a common (for simplicity) approximation.
>>>         Often a bad one. But if variances are high enough, it is
>>>         fine for most purposes.
>>>
>>>>
>>>>         The R package "lme4" allows to estimate the standard errors
>>>>         of variance components via likelihood profiling. Is it
>>>>         available in breedR?
>>>         No, it is not. You need to make ML inference for that, since
>>>         it is based on a LRT statistic.
>>>
>>>>         Isn't it what is already described in this
>>>>         <https://github.com/famuvie/breedR/wiki/Heritability#case-1-explicit-genetic-component-with-method-ai>
>>>>         wiki page as "simulation from the asymptotic Gaussian joint
>>>>         sampling distribution of the variance components" citing
>>>>         Meyer and Houle (2013)?
>>>         No, it is not the same procedure. But has the same purpose.
>>>
>>>>         If yes, could it be made available for generic variance
>>>>         components?
>>>         It is available. See case 2.1. You need to manually specify
>>>         you formula for heritability using `se_covar_function`.
>>>
>>>         Let me know if it works, or if you need any help.
>>>         I am aware that the specification of the formula is not
>>>         precisely "user-friendly" :)
>>>
